answer.exemplar: Players prefer mutual stag but fear the other will hunt hare, leaving them with nothing, so trust and coordination determine which equilibrium is played.

questions.explanation: Applying the stag hunt and risk dominance rule — Trust and coordination — yields "Players prefer mutual stag but fear the other will hunt hare, leaving them with nothing, so trust and coordination determine which equilibrium is played". Reversing the reasoning would recover the given quantities.

questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.stem: In chicken, if opponent goes Straight, your payoff for Swerve is -1 and for Straight is -5. Best response?

options.misconception: selects "Straight, because -5 is braver" instead of "Swerve, because -1 > -5"
Uses the wrong sign in swerve, because -1 is positive.
names "Indifferent, because both negative" where the rule requires "Swerve, because -1 > -5"

questions.explanation: For a chicken and asymmetric equilibrium question like this, the governing rule is: Compare -1 vs -5. Applying it makes "Swerve, because -1 > -5" correct. The alternative "Straight, because -5 is braver" is wrong because it selects "Straight, because -5 is braver" instead of "Swerve, because -1 > -5".

questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.stem: PD payoffs: T=5, R=3. Temptation to defect over cooperation when other cooperates is T-R. What is it?
questions.explanation: Temptation is 5 and the reward for cooperation is 3, so the gap is 2. That is the one-period gain from defecting while the other player cooperates, and it is what a punishment stream must outweigh.

questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.stem: A policy brief on tit-for-tat in a repeated game asks an analyst to evaluate the market evidence below. What is tit-for-tat's first move?

options.misconception: confuses with grim trigger opening? grim also cooperates
names "Match opponent's previous (none)" where the rule requires "Cooperate"

questions.explanation: Tit-for-tat opens with cooperation and then copies the opponent's previous move. Randomising has no place in it, defecting first confuses it with other strategies, and there is no previous move to match in the opening round.

questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.stem: Cooperation sustained if delta > (T-R)/(T-P). With T=4,R=2,P=0, threshold = (4-2)/(4-0)=0.5. If delta=0.6, is cooperation sustainable?

options.misconception: selects "Yes, because delta positive" instead of "Yes, because 0.6 > 0.5"
names "No, because finite horizon" where the rule requires "Yes, because 0.6 > 0.5"

questions.explanation: With a threshold of 0.5, a discount factor of 0.6 clears it, so the discounted value of future cooperation outweighs the one-off gain from defecting. Being positive is not enough, comparing the numbers the other way reverses the test, and a finite horizon is not part of this condition.

questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.stem: Stage 1: Check one-shot deviations at every history. Stage 2: If none profitable, strategy is?
questions.explanation: If no one-shot deviation is profitable at any history the strategy is subgame perfect. That is weaker than checking deviations of any length, it does establish an equilibrium, and it says nothing about dominance.

questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.stem: In a public goods game, a free rider is a player who?

options.misconception: names "Refuses to benefit" where the rule requires "Benefits from the good without contributing"
Reverses the correct ordering: contributes more than others.

options.text: Benefits from the good without contributing.

questions.explanation: The rule that settles this public goods provision game item is: Benefit without cost. That is why "Benefits from the good without contributing" is right. The option "Refuses to benefit" (names "Refuses to benefit" where the rule requires "Benefits from the good without contributing") does not satisfy the rule.

questions.stem: In a volunteer's dilemma, the mixed equilibrium has?

options.text: Each player volunteers with some probability less than one.
All players volunteer with probability one.
options.misconception: confuses "All players volunteer with probability one" with the correct "Each player volunteers with some probability less than one"
names "No one volunteers" where the rule requires "Each player volunteers with some probability less than one"

questions.explanation: Applying the volunteer's dilemma rule — Probabilistic volunteering — yields "Each player volunteers with some probability less than one". The tempting "Exactly one volunteers with certainty" fails because it confuses with pure equilibrium.

questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.stem: Stag equilibrium payoff 4, Hare equilibrium payoff 3. Payoff difference (Stag - Hare) is?
questions.explanation: 4-3=1. A stag hunt has two equilibria, and risk dominance selects the one with the larger basin of attraction under uncertainty. Assuming payoff dominance always decides is the typical mistake.

questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.stem: In chicken, mutual straight payoff -5 versus swerve 0. Loss from not swerving when other swerves is 0-(-5)? Actually payoff difference 0-(-5)=5. What is the loss?
questions.explanation: Mutual straight loses 5 relative to swerve. In chicken the asymmetric equilibria have one player swerving and the other straight, because both going straight is worst. Expecting a symmetric pure equilibrium is the common slip.

questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.stem: Explain why mutual cooperation is not a Nash equilibrium in a prisoner's dilemma.

answer.exemplar: Each player can gain by unilaterally defecting when the other cooperates, so mutual cooperation fails the no-profitable-deviation condition.

questions.explanation: The rule that settles this prisoner's dilemma item is: Deviation incentive. That is why "Each player can gain by unilaterally defecting when the other cooperates, so mutual cooperation fails the no-profitable-deviation condition" is the answer.

options.misconception: confuses "It never punishes" with the correct "It returns to cooperation after punishing a defection for one period"

options.text: It returns to cooperation after punishing a defection for one period.

options.misconception: confuses "It randomizes forgiveness" with the correct "It returns to cooperation after punishing a defection for one period"

questions.explanation: The tit-for-tat in a repeated game principle here is: One-period punishment. On that basis "It returns to cooperation after punishing a defection for one period" is correct, while "It never punishes" confuses "It never punishes" with the correct "It returns to cooperation after punishing a defection for one period".
